html:
The Māori are the Polynesian people of New Zealand, which they call Aotearoa. The map shows them from 1279, their first settlement, to 1900.

Voyagers from East Polynesia settled the islands around 1280, among the last large lands on earth to be reached by people. New Zealand was far colder than their tropical homes. Many crops failed, but the kūmara (sweet potato) grew in the north if stored over winter in pits. Huge flightless birds were easy prey, and the moa were hunted to extinction within about two centuries. People then turned more to fishing, fern root and gardens.

Society was organised in iwi (tribes) and hapū (clans). Warfare over land and resources grew, and from about 1500 people built many fortified hilltop villages, pā. Carving, weaving and facial tattoo, moko, flourished. One group went on to the Chatham Islands and became the Moriori (Moriori settle the Chathams).

The Dutch sailor Abel Tasman arrived in 1642 and left after a clash. James Cook mapped the coasts from 1769. Whalers, sealers and traders followed. Muskets brought in by trade set off the Musket Wars between tribes from about 1807. In 1814 Samuel Marsden preached the first Christian sermon in the Bay of Islands.

In 1840 many chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi with Britain. The English and Māori texts differ on what was given up. As settlers poured in and wanted land, war broke out: the New Zealand Wars lasted from 1845 to 1872. Several tribes joined the Māori King Movement from 1858 to stop land sales. The government took large areas by confiscation and through a land court. By 1896 the Māori population had fallen to about 42,000. From 1900 it began to recover. New Zealand became a dominion within the British Empire (Australia and New Zealand).
sum: The Māori are the Polynesian people of New Zealand, which they call Aotearoa. The map shows them from 1279, their first settlement, to 1900.
